papers.title: FishSense Lite: A Camera-Based, Single Laser Hardware Framework with Software System for In Situ Fish Length Measurement
papers.abstract: Fish stock assessments need fish lengths paired with species from far more places than trained surveyors can reach. Recreational divers already visit many of those places, but measuring a fish underwater has required trained observers or specialist equipment. We present FishSense Lite, which recovers fish length from a single photograph taken with a recreational dive camera, a dive laser pointer, and a 3D-printed mount. The diver aims the laser at a fish and takes a picture; afterward, the dot's position in the image gives the range to the fish, and the range turns the fish's size in the image into a length. A citizen-science program, trained by the system's builders, taught its own divers and collected lengths paired with species for 73 wild fish across seven open-water dives. On seven wild fish also measured by an underwater stereo-imaging system, the two instruments agreed without detectable bias (mean difference +0.8%). On rigid targets of known length, FishSense Lite recovered every target to within 1.3%, and 99% of 1,055 frames fell within a 15% error budget. From the error sources we measure, we derive a field protocol: calibrate against a dive slate on every dive, photograph fish within 15 degrees of perpendicular and beyond 1 m, and take at least ten frames of each.

papers.title: A Cross-Domain TARA-to-NAC Rule Mapping Methodology: From Automotive OEM Networks to Energy Storage Systems
papers.abstract: Threat analysis and risk assessment under ISO/SAE 21434 ends with cybersecurity goals, but existing methods give little structured guidance for turning those goals into enforceable network access control rules. Compliance standards such as IEC 62443, ISO/SAE 21434, and ISO/IEC 27001 are usually applied as parallel efforts rather than as one enforcement architecture. This paper presents a six-step methodology that maps cybersecurity goals from a threat analysis and risk assessment to network access control rules, each placed at a named enforcement point and traceable to the threat records behind it. It also presents a unified compliance framework that treats IEC 62443 and ISO/IEC 27001 as a fixed substrate and domain-specific regulation as an interchangeable overlay. The methodology is applied to an automotive original equipment manufacturer plant network, addressing multi-tier supplier authorization and legacy operational technology devices, and then to utility-scale battery energy storage, where North American Electric Reliability Corporation Critical Infrastructure Protection standards and ISO/IEC 27019 replace the automotive-specific standard while the substrate stays constant. In the automotive example, 37 threat entries and 24 cybersecurity goals yield 23 rules covering 11 of the 13 in-scope goals; the energy example yields six rules. Three derived rules have no equivalent in the cited standards. Both examples are desk-based: the methodology is applied to them, not tested on them. The result is a reusable pattern for translating risk assessment into enforcement across critical infrastructure sectors, with empirical validation left as future work.

papers.title: Circuit Theory-Informed AI for Condition Monitoring in Power Electronics
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence for power electronics is evolving toward a deeper comprehension of system intrinsic behaviors and dynamics. As a novel integration of neural computation and electric circuits, spike-based neuromorphic computing offers promising potential in high energy efficiency and adaptability for data-driven applications. Building on the latency-coding principles, this article proposes a framework for data-light condition monitoring that relies solely on three-phase AC current measurements. The AC current signals are encoded as membrane potentials of RC-based spiking neurons, which are inherently compatible with spiking neural networks that can effectively facilitate the estimation of device parameters. Case studies are presented to validate the performances, while constraints and further optimizations are also evaluated and discussed, and future extensions of the methodology are provided.

papers.title: Fair Selection of Generalized Nash Equilibria: A Comparability Perspective
papers.abstract: Generalized Nash equilibrium (GNE) problems model self-interested agents coupled through their costs and shared constraints, and arise throughout control applications that allocate a scarce common resource. Such problems typically admit a continuum of equilibria, so any implementation must \emph{select} one. This selection is not neutral: it decides how the cost of the shared constraint is distributed among the agents, a decision often expected to be fair. The variational GNE (v-GNE), which charges all agents a uniform shadow price, is the conventional choice and is frequently advocated as fair. Through the lens of \emph{comparability} from social choice theory, we show that the GNE set itself requires no inter-agent comparability of costs, whereas the v-GNE implicitly assumes cardinal unit comparability, one of the stronger notions. We then introduce the fair GNE (f-GNE), which selects an equilibrium by explicitly optimizing a fairness metric matched to the comparability at hand, and give constructive routes to compute it for single-constraint and linear-quadratic games. An electric-vehicle charging game serves as a running example throughout this self-contained tutorial.

papers.title: An Inspection Game for Monitor Design Against GNSS Timing Attacks in Synchronous Islanding
papers.abstract: Phasor measurement units (PMUs) take their time from GNSS, so a spoofer that slowly drags a receiver clock rotates the reported phase without touching the power waveform. The threat is acute in synchronous islanding, where a controller keeps an islanded generator in phase with the grid, using one PMU on each side of an open breaker, so that the two can be reconnected at any moment: a differential clock bias of about $0.56$\,ms can make the controller hold the generator $10^\circ$ out of phase while it reports perfect synchronism. We cast the defense as a zero-sum inspection game. The defender, as inspector, chooses its timing monitors and audits the clocks periodically; the attacker, as inspectee, drags the two clocks to an unsafe bias by the next audit; the payoff is the evidence, the Kullback--Leibler divergence between the probability laws of the defender's record under attack and under normal operation. Our central result is that the evidence equals the cost of the cheapest innocent explanation of the attacked record. This single identity predicts which monitors work, turns the attacker's best response into a strictly convex quadratic program, and turns the defender's design into a convex program with a saddle point. Pairing explanations, which bound the evidence from above, with test statistics, which bound it from below, certifies audit periods in which every successful attack leaves at least a threshold of evidence. On a 50\,Hz island, these evidence-based periods, at the matched-test threshold, are up to 8.4 times as long as those of a rule that checks each monitor separately, and the case study favors placing the better oscillator on the utility side of the breaker.

papers.title: Generative Reconstruction of Full-Field Sensor States for Safety-Critical Digital Twins
papers.abstract: Accurate reconstruction of incomplete sensor fields is critical for state awareness in safety-critical digital twins (DTs). Thermocouples in high-temperature and radiation environments may drift, fail, or become intermittently unavailable, causing partial observability. This study develops a sparse-sensor reconstruction framework for Oregon State University's High Temperature Test Facility (HTTF) and evaluates six methods under intra- and inter-experiment protocols: three conditional generative models (i.e., a diffusion model [DM], variational autoencoder [VAE], and generative adversarial network [GAN]), two deterministic recurrent neural-network models, and ridge regression. For intra-experiment reconstruction within the PG{-}29 depressurized conduction cooldown (DCC) test, the models combine graph-based spatial encoding with gated recurrent units. The graph neural network (GNN)--gated recurrent unit (GRU) VAE achieves the lowest error, with a mean absolute error (MAE) of $11.73,^\circ$C, a root mean square error (RMSE) of $20.54,^\circ$C, and an $R^2$ of 0.98. The deterministic GNN--GRU and plain GRU obtain RMSE values of $25.26,^\circ$C and $35.22,^\circ$C, respectively, demonstrating the benefit of spatial modeling. All three generative models reduce RMSE by more than half compared with ridge regression. The DM maintains an $R^2$ of 0.94 when known sensors decrease from 91 to 45. For inter-experiment reconstruction, models trained on PG{-}27 pressurized conduction cooldown (PCC) are evaluated on PG{-}29 using section-context conditioning. The section-context DM achieves the best transfer performance, with an RMSE of $42.84,^\circ$C and an $R^2$ of 0.91. These results demonstrate the value of spatiotemporal generative modeling for missing-sensor reconstruction in safety-critical DT applications.

papers.title: Sensing-Based Communication: A Non-Orthogonal Passive Reflection Framework for ISAC
papers.abstract: While integrating uplink without disrupting the primary downlink remains a critical challenge for existing reflective communication systems, this paper proposes a non-orthogonal passive integrated sensing and communication (ISAC) mechanism termed Sensing-based Communication. Originating from and validated within an optical retro-reflective system, this mechanism possesses an underlying wave-agnostic architecture with the potential to be generalized across other physical modalities. It leverages incident downlink signals for parasitic modulation via passive tags. By relying solely on fundamental on-off keying (OOK) reflection, the tag unifies the reflective sensing channel and the uplink communication channel, and simultaneously achieves both sensing and duplex communication. Consequently, our approach introduces uplink capability without sacrificing the downlink data rate or consuming additional spectrum resources. At the receiver, we design a joint decoding architecture combining cross-correlation computation and successive interference cancelation (SIC) to fully exploit the degrees of freedom in broadband signals for multi-user interference suppression. We derive closed-form expressions for the interference and bit error rate (BER) assuming zero-mean Gaussian signals. Using an experimental testbed, we validate the pivotal theoretical finding, the scaling relationship of SINR with signal bandwidth and cross-correlation time--where linear regression yields a strong goodness-of-fit with $R^2 = 0.9688$. Furthermore, evaluations under noise-like orthogonal frequency division multiplexing (OFDM) waveforms exhibit high consistency between theoretical derivations and simulation data ($R^2 = 0.9372$, mean absolute percentage error, $\text{MAPE} = 14\%$), confirming the model's accuracy and waveform generalizability.

papers.title: Extending Grid Foundation Models for Phasor-Domain Dynamic Simulation
papers.abstract: Grid Foundation Models (GridFMs) are emerging as a powerful framework for learning and transferring knowledge across power grids and grid analysis tasks. This work extends GridFMs from steady-state analysis to dynamic simulation. We present DynGridFM, which uses component-wise tokenization and a structured latent operator to learn shared dynamic representations across heterogeneous grids and enable transfer to unseen systems. Pretrained on nine grids, DynGridFM is adapted to a held-out 48-machine grid, where fine-tuning on 64 trajectories achieves accuracy comparable to training from scratch on 128. On a single GPU, it achieves 924x to 1232x speedup over numerical simulators on one CPU core.

papers.title: Grid-Oriented Probabilistic Load Forecasting for AI Data Centers
papers.abstract: Probabilistic load forecasts for AI data centers need to represent both uncertainty under changing workloads and temporal dependence to support grid operations. This paper develops an open, grid-oriented benchmark using measured GPU power from a 448-GPU AI cluster. Forecasts are evaluated through four stages: probabilistic prediction, online uncertainty calibration, temporal scenario generation, and horizon-wide reserve sizing. Following a change in cluster utilization, a quantile LightGBM forecast achieves only 63.4% coverage for a nominal 90% interval, while online regime-conditioned calibration increases coverage to 87.3%. Even with well-calibrated marginal forecasts, independent sampling produces unrealistic ramp distributions and excessive reserve procurement. Reconstructing temporal dependence from historical forecast errors reduces the discrepancy in ramp statistics and lowers realized reserve cost by 7.4-10.6% across three forecasting tasks. These findings show that marginal forecast quality alone is insufficient for operational decisions and motivate joint evaluation of calibration, temporal structure, and decision outcomes.

papers.title: Reconciling European Electricity Data with Diffusion Priors Learned from Observations Alone
papers.abstract: The ENTSO-E Transparency Platform publishes generation, load, and cross-border power flows for European bidding zones. The values carry undocumented errors and violate energy conservation, and data reconciliation consists in correcting them to satisfy that balance. In this work, we formulate data reconciliation as Bayesian inference. Classical methods implicitly take a uniform prior, which we replace with a diffusion model estimated from the observations alone by empirical-Bayes expectation-maximization. The resulting posterior is sampled with a guided process whose projection step makes every sample satisfy the balance exactly. On synthetic systems of six to thirty-five bidding zones, built from ENTSO-E resource-adequacy data, the diffusion prior gives the most accurate reconciliation, increasingly so as the system grows. Its credible intervals are calibrated or conservative, and it remains the most accurate under a misspecified noise covariance. Finally, when the generation of entire zones goes unreported, the classical methods fail while the learned prior recovers it from cross-zone structure.

papers.title: Beyond Feasibility: Efficient and Robust On-Device Localization with UWB Concurrent Transmissions
papers.abstract: Concurrent transmissions (CTX) enable an ultra-wideband (UWB) tag to range to, or self-localize from, multiple nodes with a single frame reception, significantly improving update rate and energy efficiency compared to traditional approaches. Prior work demonstrated the concept feasibility via prototypes whose real-world applicability is however hindered by many limitations, notably including their inability to directly execute on UWB tags and to cope with interfering UWB signals. We address these limitations in two ways. First, we redesign the core CTX techniques to enable a fast and efficient execution on resource-constrained MCUs without sacrificing accuracy. Second, we leverage the new features in the IEEE 802.15.4z standard to achieve robustness to interference from other UWB devices and enable tags to dynamically select which anchors to use, two crucial and unexplored capabilities in CTX-based systems. We quantitatively evaluate our approach experimentally in two real-world testbeds with different characteristics. We first analyze our new techniques individually, offering an in-depth discussion of design choices and performance trade-offs. Then, we embed all our techniques into a CTX-based system enabling a tag to self-localize entirely on-device, unlocking gains up to 44% in runtime and 85% in energy efficiency compared to traditional approaches.

papers.title: EMT Modeling and Coordinated Mode-Transition Ride-Through Control of Modern Data Centers
papers.abstract: Large data centers are emerging as power-electronic loads whose response to grid voltage disturbances can affect bulk-system stability. This paper presents the composition and control characteristics of a proprietary electromagnetic transient (EMT) model of a modern data center comprising an uninterruptible power supply (UPS) with battery energy storage, induction-motor cooling loads, a computer room air handler (CRAH) driven by a variable-frequency drive (VFD), and an aggregated server load. A voltage-based state machine coordinates three aspects of the facility response: the UPS operating mode (eco, double conversion, or battery), the supply path of the CRAH, and a ramped reconnection of the grid-side UPS converter after the disturbance clears. A 100 MW facility is implemented in PSCAD/EMTDC and benchmarked against the PSSE PERC1 aggregate data center model under a symmetrical three-phase fault and low- and high-voltage ride-through (LVRT/HVRT) events. The two models agree closely in their voltage and active-power trajectories, while the EMT model also resolves the converter and motor-reacceleration transients that the phasor-domain model cannot.

papers.title: Multi-objective Electric Vehicle Charging Strategies at Energy Hubs with Justice-informed Profit Distribution among Users
papers.abstract: This paper studies potential energy cost savings in electric vehicle (EV) charging hubs when users allow cooperative vehicle-to-grid (V2G), and how such savings should be redistributed. To this end, we present multi-objective operational strategies and justice-informed profit sharing methods for a charging energy hub equipped with a battery storage system and solar panels. Specifically, we first frame the dynamic energy hub operational problem aiming to minimize a combination of grid costs and emissions, accounting for time-varying prices and energy mix as well as storage system and EV battery degradation, which is especially relevant when considering V2G operations. We parse the problem as a second-order conic program that can be efficiently solved to global optimality. Our real-world case-study shows the importance of flexibility for hub operation: Equipping a charging station with a stationary battery and leveraging dynamic V2G can significantly reduce the total costs and emissions compared to conventional settings without a battery or dynamic charging by more than 10%. To redistribute these cost benefits to users, we compare standard Nash bargaining with a justice-informed sufficientarian version which caps charging prices to safeguard adequate access to affordable charging. Our results show that the sufficientarian approach better accounts for inequalities in flexibility capital without significantly affecting aggregate costs, highlighting how justice-informed pricing only marginally affects total revenues.

papers.title: Residential Vehicle-to-Grid Deployment: A United States-Based Stakeholder Perspective
papers.abstract: The integration of vehicle-to-grid (V2G), in which electric vehicle (EV) owners can send electricity from their vehicles back to the grid, is an emerging solution to enhance grid resilience. However, V2G deployment in the United States lags behind many other countries. This can be attributed to a broad range of factors, and to investigate them, this study analyzes semi-structured interviews with stakeholders using inductive-deductive qualitative coding. Results from the interviews are coded across financial, technical, social, political, and organizational dimensions in order to understand the three main deployment factors of drivers, benefits, and barriers of V2G. Once coded, the relationships between these factors are used to construct a cognitive map to identify actions that will most effectively drive V2G deployment. The results indicate that grid resilience and decarbonization are seen as the main benefits of V2G. User willingness to participate, a lack of technological readiness and standardization, prohibitive costs, and unsupportive laws and policies are among the most frequently cited barriers. Connections in the cognitive map indicate that the most closely related drivers for mitigating these barriers are user compensation for battery degradation, community outreach, the creation of grid interconnection standards and protocols, and supportive grants and policy frameworks for V2G piloting and adoption.

papers.title: Robust Adaptive Lyapunov-Based MPC for Nonlinear Systems with Experimental Validation on Quadcopter Attitude Control
papers.abstract: In this paper, a computationally efficient robust adaptive Lyapunov-based model predictive control (RALMPC) framework is proposed for a class of constrained nonlinear systems subject to uncertainties and external disturbances. A radial basis function neural network (RBFNN), introduced to approximate non-parametric uncertainties, is incorporated into a control Lyapunov function analysis, together with integral barrier Lyapunov functionals for state constraint enforcement. This analysis yields control and adaptation laws for parametric uncertainties, external disturbances, RBFNN weights, and worst-case approximation error, rendering the closed-loop system uniformly bounded while ensuring convergence of tracking errors to compact sets around the origin. The resulting guarantees are then embedded into the RALMPC optimal control problem through a contractive constraint, thus combining formal closed-loop stability with real-time performance optimization; at the same time, the adaptation laws allow the RALMPC prediction model to be updated online. Comparative hardware-in-the-loop simulations against state-of-the-art MPC schemes validate the efficacy and computational efficiency of the proposed framework. Ultimately, RALMPC is experimentally validated on a custom-built quadcopter platform for time-varying attitude tracking, demonstrating its practical feasibility; comparisons against alternative strategies confirm its superiority in achieving improved closed-loop performance.

papers.title: Reducing Data-Center Load Transfers with Ride-Through-Aware Voltage Control
papers.abstract: Fault-induced transfers of large data centers to backup supply can cause abrupt reductions in grid-served demand. Coordinating reactive-power support to mitigate these transfers requires consideration of facility-specific voltage--duration ride-through characteristics, particularly when support capacity is limited. This paper develops a ride-through-aware extension of quadratic voltage control that assesses voltage deviations relative to the admissible margins specified by these characteristics. We establish four design requirements that jointly express envelope-based severity, duration dependence, and preventive voltage-restoration incentives. Within a multiplicatively gated quadratic class, we derive necessary and sufficient conditions for satisfying these requirements and construct an explicit family of envelope-normalized objectives. We apply the proposed objectives to reactive-power coordination and evaluate their performance on the IEEE 14-bus, New England 39-bus, and NPCC 140-bus systems. Comparisons with Volt/VAR control, conventional nominal-voltage tracking, and recent data-center voltage-control methods demonstrate improved data-center retention under matched reactive-power support constraints. In the IEEE 14-bus study, the proposed controller reduces the mean data-center disconnection rate by 44.8\% and grid-demand loss by 27.4\% compared with the best-performing baseline. These results highlight the benefit of incorporating data-center ride-through requirements into reactive-power allocation.

papers.title: Tags Helping Tags: Coordination-Free Power Boosting for Battery-less Backscatter Networks
papers.abstract: Battery-less backscatter sensor nodes powered by radio-frequency wireless power transfer are attractive for large or hard-to-reach deployments, but their range is typically limited by the forward power-transfer link rather than by communication sensitivity. We present a method for improving power delivery, and thus range, in dense tag deployments by having nearby tags act as helpers: each helper terminates its antenna in purely reactive impedances, reflecting the power beacon's signal toward a target tag so that it combines constructively with the direct line-of-sight path and increases the power the target harvests. On a hardware testbed, helpers using discrete impedance control are shown to increase the target tag's harvested power by over 50% above an all-absorbing baseline, while randomly set helper impedances give no reliable benefit, and are sometimes even detrimental. We further propose and implement a local algorithm that lets each helper tune its own impedance using only measurements of the target's packet rate, without channel estimation or coordination between helpers, and we show that it brings the target's packet rate close to that of an independently tuned configuration. These results suggest that independent, passive sensor nodes can cooperatively extend each other's power-transfer range with minimal added infrastructure.

papers.title: Supporting Data Center Grid Integration via Co-Optimized Battery Energy Storage Sizing and Capacity Allocation
papers.abstract: Interconnecting large data centers can be delayed by grid requirements on demand flexibility, ramping limits, and ride-through performance. This paper proposes an optimization-based framework to size a Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) that accelerates data center grid integration by providing BESS capacity required to meet selected flexibility and grid-support requirements. The model co-optimizes BESS power rating and energy capacity while allocating capability across three services: (i) demand response over a specified duration, (ii) mitigation of high-magnitude, high-frequency load fluctuations through reserved active power with zero net state-of-charge change, and (iii) voltage support via reactive power capability at the point of common coupling. Minute-level operational scheduling enforces state-of-charge feasibility and load ramp constraints, and incorporates a controllable queue of delay-insensitive computing tasks to enhance flexibility. A case study using a real data center load profile demonstrates the proposed method and quantifies the BESS power-energy requirements and operational trade-offs needed to satisfy the multi-service constraints, providing practical guidance for interconnection planning and deployment.

papers.title: Safe Circumnavigation on Heterogeneous Orbits: A Range-Only HOCBF-QP Framework for Nonholonomic Multi-Agent Systems
papers.abstract: Circumnavigating a stationary target with a team of robots requires each robot to hold its own standoff distance, to stay evenly spaced from its neighbours, and to avoid collisions with the target and with each other at every instant. The task becomes arduous when the robots are assigned different orbital radii, as their sensors or roles may demand. This paper presents a safety-critical control framework for this problem. Each robot commands both its acceleration and its turn-rate, measures only its distance to the target, and exchanges information only with its two ring neighbours. The design has three features. First, a structural property of the model lets one control law serve every robot regardless of its assigned radius. Second, the acceleration drives each radius exactly to its target, while the turn-rate balances the formation with the neighbours. Third, a higher-order control-barrier-function quadratic program enforces target, geofence, and inter-robot safety on both inputs at once; it leaves the nominal controller untouched away from the constraints and stays valid while the unmeasured range rate is still being estimated. Simulations confirm these guarantees. In a comparison, the closest existing multi-orbit design, even with full state information, violates both the target standoff and the inter-robot margin, whereas the proposed controller does not.

papers.title: Controlled Excitation for Identification of Nonlinear Systems with Saturated Outputs
papers.abstract: We consider nonlinear systems whose measured output is the product of an unknown matrix and a known saturation function of the unmeasured state. Generating excitation that allows the matrix to be recovered from the output is challenging when the dynamics are largely unknown. We exploit saturation to construct this excitation. Under a geometric accessibility condition, we derive explicit open-loop controls that drive the state into regions where the saturation takes prescribed values. For componentwise saturations, this condition holds generically with as few as two independent control directions. The controls require no state measurement and only partial knowledge of the dynamics, with no information on the structure of its nonlinear part. The resulting regressor is known in advance, and the unknown matrix is recovered exactly by a closed-form regression. Under stronger structural assumptions and with sufficiently many independent outputs, an output feedback tracks prescribed reference trajectories within the unsaturated region to arbitrary accuracy and permits exact state recovery. Suitably chosen references then also enable exact identification of linearly parameterized (nonlinear) dynamics. We analyze robustness to measurement noise and illustrate the method numerically in the presence of both measurement and dynamical noise.

papers.title: DC-Link Voltage Regulation in a Single-Isolation-Stage Multioutput Solid-State Transformer for Wide-Range DC Outputs
papers.abstract: Single-isolation-stage solid-state transformers with balancing circuits eliminate an additional downstream dc--dc conversion stage. However, the remaining isolated converters must directly accommodate a wide output-voltage range. This paper investigates variable dc-link voltage operation of a single-isolation-stage multioutput SST to ease this requirement. Coordinated cascaded H-bridge modulation and embedded four-switch balancing circuits support intentionally unequal submodule dc-link voltages, allowing the isolated-converter input voltages to be adjusted according to the output requirements. The achievable voltage range is determined by relating the required balancing power to the BC transfer capability within the available CHB switching windows, subject to modulation and peak and rms current limits. The analysis quantifies the range extension provided by BC operation beyond modulation alone. For a single-phase-shift dual-active-bridge converter, input-voltage following within this range reduces the calculated peak current and extends the ideal zero-voltage-switching region compared with fixed input. Experiments on a six-submodule SST prototype demonstrate unequal dc-link voltage operation and inter-submodule power exchange. Experiments result on DAB demonstrate reduced current stress and improved efficiency with voltage following.

papers.title: An Optimal Power-Flow Grouping Topology for Single-Isolation-Stage Multi-Output Solid-State Transformers
papers.abstract: Electric-vehicle dc fast-charging stations and data centers require multiple high-power dc outputs with independently varying demands. Conventional multi-output solid-state transformers typically establish a common dc bus and use downstream dc/dc converters for port-level regulation and, where required, galvanic isolation. A single-isolation-stage solid-state transformer can eliminate this additional high-power interface stage by directly forming multiple isolated outputs from its submodule dc/dc stages. However, because one submodule is generally insufficient for an individual output port, multiple submodules must be connected in parallel, while inter-submodule balancing circuits redistribute power under unbalanced loading. The submodule grouping therefore determines the internal balancing-power paths. Sequential grouping can create long transfer paths and accumulated balancing power, increasing current stress and losses. This paper proposes an optimal power-flow grouping topology that interleaves submodules assigned to different output ports, thereby localizing power redistribution and reducing the power processed by the balancing circuits. Analytical models quantify the required balancing power and its reduction relative to sequential grouping. A coordinated submodule-bypass strategy is also developed, and the remaining output-power capability under different fault scenarios is evaluated. A six-submodule prototype validates the proposed topology. Under the same highly unbalanced operating conditions, the proposed topology reduces the maximum submodule dc-link voltage difference by 63\% and the peak balancing current by 14.5%, while improving the measured efficiency by approximately 5.6% at rated power. Stable post-fault operation is also experimentally demonstrated.

papers.title: Characterization of the Frequency-Current Curve of First-Order High-Pass Neurons
papers.abstract: A spiking model, called the High-Pass (HP) model, has recently been proposed as a minimal excitable primitive. This model is composed of a static activation function, usually a sigmoid, in positive feedback with a high-pass filter. The HP model enters a tonic spiking regime whenever its input lies in the high-gain zone of the sigmoid, where the sigmoid's slope exceeds 1. In neuroscience, the frequency-current (FI) curve is the standard way of characterizing the tonic spiking regime of a neuron. So far, the FI curve of the HP model has been characterized analytically only for specific sigmoids, and has otherwise been computed through simulation. These simulations are computationally heavy, since simulating neurons requires solving a stiff system of differential equations. This paper bridges this gap by analytically characterizing the FI curve of the HP model with a first-order high-pass filter, for a broad class of sigmoid functions. The FI curve of the first-order HP model can be computed by solving two input-independent equations and evaluating two input-dependent integrals, with no need to simulate the model itself. A spiking primitive is said to be Type I (resp. Type II) if tonic spiking starts at a zero (resp. non-zero) frequency. This paper also shows that, for the HP model, the type depends solely on the local shape of the sigmoid at the outer edges of its high-gain zone. A sharp corner, where the derivative approaches a value strictly smaller than 1 from the outside, yields a Type I primitive. A locally twice differentiable corner, with a bounded second derivative and a derivative approaching 1 at the edge, yields a Type II primitive.

papers.title: A Novel Algorithm to Simulate Conductance-based Neuronal Networks
papers.abstract: Conductance-based models are central to neurophysiology and neuromorphic engineering, yet their simulation scales poorly to large networks. We study and analyze an iterative solver that operates in signal space. Each iteration reduces to $N$ decoupled scalar linear time-varying differential equations, one per neuron, which are solved in parallel and in closed form. The solver admits two complementary interpretations: a variable metric forward-backward splitting method, rooted in operator theory, and a waveform relaxation quasi-Newton method, rooted in circuit simulation. We prove uniform and superlinear convergence, with a bound that reflects the conductance structure of the dynamics. The algorithm is illustrated on the classical Hodgkin--Huxley neuron and on networks of up to 5000 neurons.

papers.title: LACART: Lookahead-Augmented Collision Avoidance and Reference Tracking Strategies for Safety-Critical Robots
papers.abstract: Autonomous racing provides a demanding testbed for collision avoidance under tight geometric and computational constraints. Building on a recent conference contribution and a master's dissertation, LACART combines lookahead-based control barrier functions (CBFs), a relaxed control Lyapunov function (CLF), and quadratic programming (QP) to modify nominal vehicle commands for obstacle avoidance and reference tracking. The method handles circular obstacles and track boundaries in a common optimisation layer. Comparative simulation results against Huang \emph{et al.} \cite{r9} show similar full-track paths and lower median computation times: 0.31 versus 0.33 ms per step and 0.023 versus 0.025 ms per QP solve. The dissertation further demonstrates a 1:43-scale vehicle with camera-based estimation and wireless actuation at a reported 25 Hz control rate. We identify the conditions linking lookahead-point clearance to body clearance, illustrate hardware limitations, and propose a recorded demonstration of safety intervention and recovery. The contribution targets ground-robot collision avoidance and real-time safety monitoring.

papers.title: Nonlinear Fault Tolerant Control of Wind Turbine Pitch Systems: A Comparative Study
papers.abstract: Electro-hydraulic pitch systems account for about one fifth of wind-turbine failures, motivating the development of resilient control strategies for fault mitigation. The study considers a large set of robust nonlinear control designs of different feedback principles and architectures, and assesses their fault-tolerant capabilities in comparison to each other and against the industrial standard, i.e. the Proportional-Integral (PI) controller. The implementation and tuning of each scheme is based on a high-fidelity simulator to ensure nominal performance, whereas each controller is deployed unchanged on an experimental apparatus that includes a full-scale electro-hydraulic pitch system. The comparative evaluation of the considered fault-tolerant solutions is carried out through several tests that cover nominal operation and twenty-five representative fault scenarios, including sensor, process, and actuator faults. The analysis highlights the trade-off between performance preservation under faults and increased actuator chattering. The experimental results show that introducing a dynamic input-reconstruction module into the design of the nonlinear controllers significantly reduces actuator chatter without compromising their fault-tolerant properties.

papers.title: Adaptive PD-like Fault Tolerant Controller for a Class of Nonlinear Systems
papers.abstract: The article presents a nonlinear adaptive control strategy for a class of feedback-linearizable systems subject to process faults and disturbance. The controller is derived through Lyapunov analysis and incorporates an adaptive proportional gain within a PD-like structure, preserving simplicity while providing nonlinear adaptive behavior. A residual-based gating mechanism activates the adaptation only when the tracking error exceeds a prescribed threshold, preventing unnecessary gain updates during nominal operation and improving robustness to noise. The proposed design yields uniform global ultimate boundedness of the closed-loop signals, with explicit expressions for the steady-state tracking bound. Practical tuning guidelines for the adaptive parameters and Lyapunov matrix selection are provided to ensure consistent gating behavior. Simulations on a precision positioning system illustrate effective compensation of process faults, rapid gain escalation during degraded conditions, and smooth reversion to nominal performance, demonstrating that the method enhances fault tolerance while retaining the structural simplicity of PD control.

papers.title: Autonomous Whole-body Loco-manipulation Using a Snake Robot
papers.abstract: Snake robots can leverage their hyper-redundant morphology for both locomotion and manipulation through distributed body contact but whole-body loco-manipulation is particularly challenging since the entire body serves simultaneously as propulsive mechanism and manipulation tool Prior work on wheeled legged and snake robot platforms has decoupled these functions through dedicated appendages body segmentation or grippers We present closed-loop loco-manipulation with our snake robot COBRA without this distinction such that any part of the body may make contact We develop a contact-implicit dynamic model unifying robot-ground robot-object and object-ground interactions within a Moreau-Jean time-stepping framework and formulate a trajectory optimization over the full-order dynamics guided by a geometric planner and nominal proportional controller to autonomously push an object to a goal location during sidewinding We validate the planner and controller on hardware across varied configurations and present simulation results for a simplified trajectory optimization that resolves robot-object and object-ground contacts

papers.title: Generalized H matrix stability for power systems
papers.abstract: The small-signal stability of a power system model with arbitrary loads is investigated, with a focus on locally constant power loads in lossless networks. A central element of the proposed analysis is the matrix H, which represents the partial derivatives of generator powers with respect to their relative angles. The local stability of any equilibrium point is determined by the properties of H if the loads consume locally constant power. Specifically, an equilibrium point is asymptotically stable if H is positive definite and unstable if H is full-rank and not positive definite, while several quantitative relationships between the eigenvalues of H and the system Jacobian matrix are also established. The main contribution is that loads are allowed to be arbitrarily located within the transmission network, thereby generalizing the existing H matrix stability criterion which is valid only if loads are located at the same buses as the generators. The advantage of the proposed criterion is demonstrated through case studies involving systems with up to 2869 buses. Accurate stability assessments are maintained, where alternative methods, such as the NRPS model, are found to be overly conservative. Additionally, a computational acceleration by a factor of 340 relative to Jacobian-based methods is achieved.

papers.title: Spiking neuromodulation: a linear control perspective
papers.abstract: Neuronal excitability is a nonlinear phenomenon, and the complexity of spiking experimental traces sometimes looks defeating. The present paper takes the view point that excitability is a neuromodulated property, and aims to demonstrate that the neuromodulation of spiking is amenable to the classical linear analysis tools of control theory. We illustrate the value of linear feedback analysis as an alternative to bifurcation analysis in the simple yet classical example of spiking modulation by the A-type potassium current.
